Introduction Advanced Therapeutic Medicinal Products (ATMPs), including stem cells, extracellular vesicles (EVs), and mitochondria, are at the forefront of biomedical research, offering potential cures for previously untreatable diseases [ – ]. These innovative “Living Drugs” (LDs) are distinguished by their dynamic adaptability to the complex biological signals of damage within patients. This adaptability can lead to phenotypic changes, influencing their therapeutic effectiveness [ , ]. Their unique capability to be tailored to individual patient needs and to be engineered in vitro for specific therapeutic actions heralds a new era in medicine and healthcare [ , ]. Nonetheless, the development of LDs is intricate, necessitating rigorous techniques, a framework, definitions, and a deep conceptual grasp to navigate the challenges they present. Such an understanding is pivotal for clinicians, researchers, regulators, and investors as they work together to substantiate the efficacy and safety of these therapies [ – ]. In this review, we strive to delineate a definition for LDs, underlining the imperative to distinguish them from conventional biological products. The latter are generally simpler in production and do not typically involve or allow for the modification of genetic material, nor do they possess the innate ability to react uniquely to an individual patient’s biological milieu [ , ]. Despite the European Medicines Agency (EMA) and the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) making strides in classifying Advanced Therapeutic Medicinal Products (ATMPs)— including somatic cell therapy medicinal products (SCTMP), tissue-engineered products (TEP), gene therapy medicinal products (GTMP), and combined ATMPs (cATMPs)—there is a necessity for more granular regulatory guidelines. The existing definitions and categorizations of advanced therapies in the EU and US require further refinement to enhance guidance for the scientific and medical communities in their research and clinical applications. We posit that a well-articulated definition of LDs is essential for fulfilling the evolving demands of the burgeoning network of professionals pioneering in this domain. For instance, chimeric antigen receptor T (CAR T) cells, while classified as GTMPs as per European regulation 1394/2007 [ ] have intricate processes of production, distribution, and application that call for a specialized framework, aligning more closely with SCTMPs due to their distinct operational requirements and their divergence from other gene therapy products [ ]. While this article recognizes the broad spectrum of ATMPs that align with the definition of LDs, our focus narrows to mitochondria. We explore key aspects of its development and application as a therapeutic product, from the process of isolating mitochondria from donor cells to their subsequent artificial transfer or transplantation (AMT/T) into recipient cells or tissues in distress, evaluating their restorative potential and suitability as LDs. Mitochondria, traditionally celebrated as the cellular powerhouses, are now appreciated as dynamic signaling organelles within a mitochondrial information processing system (MIPS), engaging in constant communication with the nucleus and other organelles. Their roles extend beyond ATP synthesis; mitochondria are key players in biosynthesis and critical cellular functions essential for cell survival and activity [ ]. The natural mitochondrial transfer (NMT) that occurs from mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) to cells under stress, for instance, highlights their inherent reparative capabilities. These capabilities, coupled with advancements in mitochondrial biology, are paving the way for the adoption of mitochondria through AMT/T as a novel class of LDs [ , ]. The goal of AMT/T is to rejuvenate and restore compromised cellular and tissue functions—an innovative approach still in its nascent stages [ , – ]. Our aim is to contribute to the growing repository of knowledge on mitochondria’s application as LDs and their potential in regenerative medicine. We highlight in our article how mitochondria have emerged as potent therapeutic tools with the potential to address a broad spectrum of medical challenges. This article takes a novel approach by examining the definition of LDs and how mitochondria align with this concept, especially within the context of emerging companies engaged in clinical trials. We provide a much-needed overview of the recent evidence supporting the therapeutic use of mitochondria, delving into the work of pioneering companies such as Cellvie, Dragon BioMed, LUCA Science, Mitobridge, Mitrix Bio, Minovia Therapeutics, and Yuva Bioscience. While the use of stem cells, extracellular vesicles (EVs), and other biological constructs has been well-documented, the specific application of AMT/T remains underexplored. This article seeks to fill that void by providing a comprehensive examination of the unique characteristics, potential origins, and key regulatory considerations of mitochondria as LDs, alongside highlighting the burgeoning interest from the pharmaceutical sector. Currently, the integration of mitochondria as LDs into therapeutic protocols lacks definitive guidance from regulatory bodies such as the EMA and FDA. Despite this regulatory vacuum, there is a discernible surge of interest from both scientific researchers and industry stakeholders to establish the safety and efficacy of mitochondrial therapies. Currently, the integration of mitochondria as LDs into therapeutic protocols lacks definitive guidance from regulatory bodies such as the EMA and FDA. Despite this regulatory vacuum, there is a discernible surge of interest from both scientific researchers and industry stakeholders to establish the safety and efficacy of mitochondrial therapies. Considering the emerging recognition of mitochondrial function in cell and tissue recuperation, coupled with keen industrial engagement and the absence of a solid regulatory framework, this work is positioned at a critical juncture. Our aim is to contribute a foundational conceptual framework and definition for LDs, championing the role of mitochondria as a significant and promising category within this innovative therapeutic class. 2. Defining the concept of “Living Drugs” (LDs) Historically, “LDs” was a term primarily attributed to genetically-engineered cells boasting supra-physiological properties. They held paramount significance in the realm of biological and adoptive cell therapies, with cancer as a prime target [ , ]. Typically, the source cells for LDs are procured from donor tissues or from healthy volunteers after securing informed consent. Post-harvesting, these cells undergo a meticulous regimen of culturing, expansion, and genetic modification. The nature and objective of these genetic alterations are condition-specific. For instance, certain LDs are crafted to express cancer antigen-specific chimeric antigen receptors (CAR) or T-cell receptors (TCR) [ ]. Once introduced into a patient, these bioengineered LDs display a propensity to proliferate and establish themselves within the host. Through antigenic stimuli, they can specifically target tumor cells or activate other therapeutic modalities [ ]. Recent innovations have steered the spotlight towards CAR natural killer cells and macrophages. These are now under clinical trials as potential therapeutic interventions against solid tumors [ , , ]. Venturing beyond these typical examples, the LD spectrum is vast. Mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs), for instance, are making waves. The prevailing paradigm is shifting from utilizing MSCs themselves to tapping into their extracellular vesicles (EVs). Such strategic transitions aim at reducing therapeutic variability and ensuring consistent outcomes. This evolution towards cell-free therapies heralds a new era in regenerative medicine [ , ]. Furthermore, the innate ability of MSCs to transfer mitochondria to stressed or damaged cells is gaining attention. By replenishing cells with healthy mitochondria, there is potential to ensure long-term tissue vitality [ , , , , ]. This concept of transferring mitochondria from MSCs to ailing cells paves the way for an innovative cell-free therapeutic category within LDs. Moreover, other examples of LDs include dendritic cells (used in cancer vaccines) [ ], virus-specific T cells (to combat viral infections post-transplantation) [ ], and regulatory T cells (for autoimmune conditions and transplant rejection prevention) [ ]. Each of these LD variants offers unique mechanisms of action and therapeutic benefits. Given these insights and the need of the biomedical and ATMPs field, we present a comprehensive and refined definition for “Living Drugs”: Living Drugs (LDs) are versatile biological entities derived from various anatomical origins. They can be whole cells or specialized subcellular components that are amenable to ex vivo culture and expansion, precise genetic engineering, and therapeutic delivery. Their defining features include possessing genetic material suitable for modification that directs protein synthesis or other regulatory functions. This can impart temporary or enduring therapeutic effects, be tailored for functional modification or enhancement, or introduce novel capabilities to address the needs of individual patients or specific patient populations. Once inside the patient, they are capable of dynamically responding to the extracellular or intracellular environment, with the potential to persist over time, proliferate and even evolve ( ). To further demarcate what qualifies as an LD, we believe that cells or tissues undergoing minimal manipulation, and used in autologous or homologous therapies, should be exempt from this classification. Examples like autologous hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (auto-HSCT), autologous chondrocytes, and epithelial cells grafted onto synthetic matrices fall into this category [ , ]. We believe that cells or tissues undergoing minimal manipulation, and used in autologous or homologous therapies, should also be exempt from this classification. Furthermore, AMT/T involving mitochondria isolated from muscle or other tissues and used in the same patient, should not be deemed LDs. This stance is taken despite the method’s accessibility and potential as a therapeutic agent [ ]. Examples like autologous hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (auto-HSCT), autologous chondrocytes, and epithelial cells grafted onto synthetic matrices fall into this category and outside the concept of LDs. The evolving landscape of biopharmaceuticals, especially the emergence of LDs, highlights the necessity of this concept in the scientific and medical community. This stance is taken despite the method’s accessibility and potential as a therapeutic agent [ ]. Examples like autologous hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (auto-HSCT), autologous chondrocytes, and epithelial cells grafted onto synthetic matrices fall into this category and outside the concept of LDs. The evolving landscape of biopharmaceuticals, especially the emergence of LDs, highlights the necessity of this concept in the scientific and medical community. Establishing this concept, as elucidated in our discussions, is pivotal for streamlining research, clinical applications, and regulatory approvals. Instituting a robust regulatory framework that hinges on this defined concept would provide clarity and direction to researchers and clinicians but also safeguards patients’ health by upholding highest quality standards based on the characteristics of LDs and the complexity of their development. Essential to this endeavor are good manufacturing practices (GMPs) and tissue and cell directives that oversee every facet of the transplant process—from donation, procurement, and testing to processing, preservation, storage, and distribution. Moreover, an integrated risk management plan becomes key to ensure every potential adverse scenario is anticipated and addressed. With a clear concept of LDs as the foundation, a comprehensive and stringent regulatory environment becomes achievable. 3. From MSCs to the use of mitochondria as novel LDs Having defined the concept of LDs, we now focus on one of the most innovative therapeutic strategies in development: AMT/T. This approach marks a revolutionary transition in regenerative medicine, emphasizing the utilization of inherent reparative mechanisms within cellular organelles, rather than deploying whole cells. MSCs are renowned for their therapeutic properties, notably their ability to generate EVs and facilitate mitochondrial transfer or NMT to cells under duress, effectively replenishing the mitochondrial pool in recipient cells and restoring their functional capabilities [ , , ]. The natural transfer of mitochondria between cells, such as from platelets to MSCs or from MSCs to cancer cells, can induce the reprogramming of metabolic functions as well as promote proliferation and migration [ , ]. Moreover, mitochondria have been observed to exist in various extracellular forms, and their presence may be crucial for maintaining or restoring overall health [ , , – ]. Transient cellular connections, such as tunneling nanotubes (TnTs), along with extracellular vesicle-associated mitochondria and the release of free mitochondria, are mechanisms for NMT [ , , , ]. MSCs, for instance, can unidirectionally transfer mitochondria to cardiomyocytes in co-culture, aiding in myocardial repair [ , ]. Similarly, bone marrow-derived stromal cells (BMSCs) have demonstrated the ability to transfer mitochondria to alveolar cells, providing protection against acute lung injury (ALI) [ ]. Neuronal mitochondrial donation to astrocytes, and vice versa, has also been documented [ , ]. Furthermore, macrophages can receive mitochondria from adipocytes, suggesting a pursuit to achieve metabolic homeostasis. Moreover, macrophages have been observed to receive mitochondria from adipocytes, which is suggestive of a regulatory mechanism for metabolic homeostasis. Notably, obesity has been linked to reduced mitochondrial transfer to macrophages, where adipocytes release mitochondria into the bloodstream, triggering a protective antioxidant response in the heart [ , ]. Even within the context of cancer, mitochondrial transfer plays a role: MSCs from the bone marrow have been shown to donate these organelles to tumor cells, supporting their growth [ ], and there is evidence of mitochondrial exchange between cancerous and non-cancerous cells within the tumor microenvironment [ ]. These instances of NMT have prompted scientists, clinicians, and biotechnology firms to investigate various applications of AMT/T, aiming to develop new treatments that range from targeting the nervous system to repairing tissue damage, which could enhance health outcomes in several ways [ , , ]. Initial experiments involving the AMT/T into recipient mammalian cells date back to 1982 and were reportedly conducted by Clark and Shay [ ]. Subsequent investigations expanded upon this principle by utilizing microinjection techniques to introduce isolated mitochondria into cell lines and mouse ova [ , ]. Interestingly, Singh and Weissig’s team achieved successful xenogenic transfer of murine mitochondria into human cells lacking functional mitochondria, resulting in the restoration of respiratory function and the introduction of exogenous DNA into mammalian mitochondria [ ]. Since then, the field has progressed from in vitro and in vivo assays to clinical trials. Numerous AMT/T companies have emerged, working on the further development of this evolving therapeutic option to capitalize on the various forms of mitochondria and their therapeutic potential. In the past four decades, the AMT/T process has encompassed various specific terms, such as mitochondrial augmentation therapy (MAT), MitoCeption, MitoT (mitochondrial transfer), mitochondrial transplant, Magnetomitotransfer, MitoPunch (a device for delivering isolated mitochondria into multiple target mammalian cells simultaneously), and others [ , – ]. Numerous AMT/T companies have emerged, working on the further development of this evolving therapeutic option to capitalize on the various forms of mitochondria and their therapeutic potential. In the past four decades, the AMT/T process has encompassed various specific terms, such as mitochondrial augmentation therapy (MAT), MitoCeption, MitoT (mitochondrial transfer), mitochondrial transplant, Magnetomitotransfer, MitoPunch (a device for delivering isolated mitochondria into multiple target mammalian cells simultaneously), and others [ , – ]. AMT/T holds great potential for treating wounded tissue and curing or preventing diseases or tissue exhaustion associated with aging [ , , , , – ]. Notably, AMT/T can utilize mitochondria isolated from diverse cell sources, obtain them in scalable quantities, and administer them ex vivo, intravenously, in situ, or even intranasally, in an autologous or non-autologous manner. In this context, isolated mitochondria can be regarded as biological drugs or LDs [ , , – ]. Since mitochondria possess their own DNA and can remain “alive or viable” outside the cell, they could be considered LDs. Further insights will be discussed in the next section. 4. Why mitochondria could be considered as an LD An LD represents an advanced biological product, distinguished by its living nature, adaptability, and the ability for precise customization to meet therapeutic objectives. This innovative approach signifies a departure from traditional pharmaceuticals towards a more dynamic, personalized medicine model. According to the concept introduced in this article, a cell or subcellular product must fulfill several key criteria to be classified as an LD. When applying the LD concept to mitochondria for use in AMT/T, we find: LDs are inherently biological entities, ranging from complete cells to cell-derived components like mitochondria. Considering the diverse characteristics of LDs, mitochondria make a strong case for their inclusion in this category. Mitochondria retain their own genetic material, mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA), which encodes for 13 polypeptides [ , , , ]. This mtDNA functions with a partial degree of autonomy from the cell nucleus and can coordinate together the expression of more than 200 genes, crucial for mitochondrial replication, transcription, and repair processes. Furthermore, mitochondria with distinct mtDNA profiles are capable of eliciting a variety of changes after transfer in recipient cells, potentially enhancing their resilience to adverse external factors ( ) [ , , ]. Once recipient cells take up mitochondria through a mechanism mediated by the heparan sulfate (HS) biosynthetic pathway [ ], these organelles can dynamically interact with the cytoplasmic environment and existing mitochondria within the recipient [ ]. Mitochondria’s dynamic responsiveness to environmental changes underscores their adaptability [ ]. They can modify their physiological functions, such as metabolic pathways, to meet cellular demands and protect the cells against various stressors, an attribute that aligns with the defining characteristics of LDs [ , ]. Moreover, mitochondria are involved in critical signaling pathways, actively communicating with other cellular compartments, thus influencing cell survival, differentiation, and growth [ – ]. It has been documented that both functional and depolarized mitochondria ejected by MSCs can be repurposed via mitochondrial fusion, thereby augmenting bioenergetics in macrophages [ ]. Interestingly, it has been observed that the transfer of a specific type of mitochondria can induce cellular changes, prompting cells to increase mitochondrial biogenesis and, in turn, transfer another type of mitochondria. For instance, mitochondria released from damaged somatic cells can activate MSCs to deliver healthy mitochondria to dying cells. This suggests that transferred mitochondria can integrate into the recipient cell’s metabolic processes and possibly its mitochondrial network. Such integration, which includes contributing genetic material, has the potential to alter the metabolism and cellular properties of the recipient cells [ ]. Intriguingly, different mitochondria can induce diverse outcomes, such as enhanced mitochondrial biogenesis, increased oxidative phosphorylation capacity, and cell proliferation [ , ]. The ability to select a specific cell as a mitochondrial donor, or to modify donor cells or isolated mitochondria before its extraction to induce targeted effects in the recipient cells or tissues [ , ], underscores their potential as an LD ( ). For practical and clinical applications, LDs must be conducive to ex-vivo cultivation and expansion ( – ). This scalability is crucial for generating adequate quantities for therapeutic dosing and enables quality control and standardization [ ]. However, this pivotal step necessitates stringent conditions and adherence to GMPs, which ensure the safety and efficacy of the product for patient application [ ]. For instance, in the context of CAR T cells therapies, the expansion of modified cells prior to patient administration is a critical process that is rigorously controlled and monitored to preserve cell quality [ ]. It involves the cultivation of cells in a high number before isolation, or the eventual growth of mitochondria with specified characteristics ( ). The therapeutic potential of mitochondria is noteworthy. Through AMT/T, mitochondria can be harnessed to rejuvenate damaged cells, restore normal cellular functions, and even modulate immune responses [ – , , ]. Their utility spans a wide range of pathological conditions, from degenerative diseases to tissue repair and management of mitochondrial dysfunction disorders [ , , ]. The aspect of precision and personalization in therapy, central to the LD concept, also finds resonance with mitochondrial interventions. Isolated mitochondria, whether autologous or allogeneic, can be specifically chosen or modified for a patient, based on the underlying pathology and individual cellular requirements. These mitochondrial preparations can be administered through various routes, ensuring targeted delivery and optimal therapeutic outcomes ( ). In conclusion, based on their inherent biological properties, functional versatility, and the capacity for therapeutic modulation, mitochondria fit the criteria of LDs. Their integration into the classification of ATMPs represents a novel, promising avenue that transcends the limitations of traditional pharmaceuticals, offering a more dynamic, tailored approach to disease management and recovery ( ). 5. Development of mitochondria as a “Living Drug,” insights from the industry Transitioning from laboratory research to clinical applications, the utilization of mitochondria as LDs has amassed compelling evidence supporting their capacity to address diseases and facilitate tissue regeneration ( – ). Even though our comprehension of the intricate mechanisms governing the entry of extracellular mitochondria into cells and their role in metabolic reprogramming remains incomplete, this knowledge gap has not dissuaded companies from actively pursuing the development of therapies aimed at harnessing the regenerative and therapeutic potential of mitochondria in the form of LDs. In the subsequent section, we will delve into the prevalent applications of AMT/T as pursued by these companies, drawing insights from their official websites and additional sources referenced within this article. Various companies and initiatives, including Cellvie, Dragon BioMed, LUCA Science, Mitobridge, Mitrix Bio, Minovia Therapeutics, and Yuva Bioscience, are actively exploring the application of mitochondria as a safe and effective therapeutic option. It is important to note that this list is not exhaustive; there may be additional firms contributing to this field. Several are engaged in clinical trials, investigating exciting new uses for mitochondria as LDs. Non-inherited mitochondrial disorders are rare pediatric diseases caused by mutations in the mtDNA leading to a systemic multi-organ disease and possibly death of the patient [ ]. Currently, there is a lack of effective treatments to cure these diseases, necessitating the exploration of new therapeutic options. Determining the prevalence of these diseases is challenging due to clinical and genetic heterogeneity among patients [ ]. The phenotypic spectrum of mtDNA diseases has significantly expanded with the study of mtDNA rearrangements, point mutations, and further understanding of the severity of symptoms [ ]. Furthermore, the cost of treating these diseases represents a burden for both patients and society, underscoring the need for innovative therapeutic approaches [ , ]. An example of the development of treatments for both inherited and non-inherited primary mtDNA diseases is the utilization of Mitochondria Augmentation Therapy (MAT) [ ]. MAT is currently being employed for the ex-vivo transfer of exogenous mitochondria to hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells (HSPCs) [ ]. Research has demonstrated that MAT is feasible, dosage-dependent, and enhances mitochondrial content and respiration in both healthy HSPCs and those affected by mitochondrial diseases [ ]. The objective of this process is to alleviate the symptoms of mitochondrial disorders, with the potential to serve as a disease-modifying therapy for mtDNA disorders [ ]. Collaborating with prominent medical centers in Israel, MAT developers have published two studies focusing on its application. Their initial publication, titled “First-in-Human Mitochondrial Augmentation of Hematopoietic Stem Cells in Pearson Syndrome,” was released in 2018 and reported the enrichment of hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) with healthy mitochondria resulting in improved metabolism, aerobic capacity, and enhanced quality of life for patients [ ]. Israel, MAT developers have published two studies focusing on its application. Their initial publication, titled “First-in-Human Mitochondrial Augmentation of Hematopoietic Stem Cells in Pearson Syndrome,” was released in 2018 and reported the enrichment of hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) with healthy mitochondria resulting in improved metabolism, aerobic capacity, and enhanced quality of life for patients [ ]. In 2021, the MAT developers published a second paper titled “Mitochondrial augmentation of CD34 + cells from healthy donors and patients with mitochondrial DNA disorders confers a functional benefit.” This study provided additional insights into the application of MAT in various cell types, including human peripheral blood-derived CD34 + cells, human cord blood CD34 + cells, and murine bone marrow cells. The researchers observed that the benefits of MAT were dependent on the dosage administered to the affected cells and patients. Notably, they also demonstrated that exogenous mitochondria derived from MAT cells could be transferred to other cell types, resulting in systemic metabolic benefits, even in individuals without mitochondrial diseases [ ]. MAT is currently undergoing evaluation for the treatment of both inherited and non-inherited primary mtDNA diseases through three clinical trials [ – ]. One of these trials, NCT03384420 (MNV-BM-BLD), was initiated in 2017 and focuses on pediatric patients with Pearson Syndrome. The aim is to treat these patients by enriching their autologous hematopoietic stem cells with healthy mitochondria obtained from donor blood cells [ ]. For patients with inherited mitochondrial diseases, MAT developers are assessing the safety of a single intravenous (IV) infusion of autologous CD34 + cells enriched with placenta-derived allogeneic mitochondria [ ]. This evaluation is being conducted in participants with primary mitochondrial diseases associated with mtDNA deletions [ ]. Another trial, NCT04548843 (MNV-BM-PLC), is a phase I clinical trial that commenced in 2020, utilizing placenta as a source to isolate healthy mitochondria for MAT [ ]. Furthermore, the clinical trial NCT03762512 , initiated in 2018, aimed to collect placenta for mitochondria isolation. This trial considered various measurements, including placenta weight and the mother’s health during pregnancy, to assess the effectiveness of placenta as a mitochondria source compared to other tissues [ ]. The ex-vivo application of AMT/T to cells has the potential to induce therapeutic reprogramming, resulting in changes that restore health following the infusion in patients [ ]. As mentioned previously, the utilization of MAT in hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) for treating Pearson Syndrome serves as an example of the diverse applications of AMT/T. Techniques such as MAT and MitoCeption offer attractive options for private initiatives interested in utilizing mitochondria from various tissue sources and cells, particularly MSCs. MitoCeption (EP3169338A1) enables the direct and quantitative transfer of mitochondria isolated from any cell type or tissue to recipient cells [ ]. Moreover, not only can a single source of mitochondria be utilized, but a mixture of mitochondria from multiple healthy donors can also rescue stressed cells in an ex-vivo model subjected to ultraviolet radiation (UVR) [ ]. Additionally, the transfer of mitochondria to Th17 cells has been shown to induce an immune regulatory profile, suggesting the potential for treating rheumatic diseases [ ]. Ischemia/reperfusion injury (I/R or IRI) plays a crucial role in conditions such as myocardial infarction, ischemic stroke, acute kidney injury (AKI), trauma, and organ transplantation, all of which have a significant negative impact on patient survival [ – ]. During an IRI event, blood flow to the tissue is interrupted and subsequently restored, directly impairing mitochondrial function [ ]. Currently, AMT/T is being investigated as a potential treatment for IRI. Both preclinical and clinical evidence primarily focus on the autologous use of mitochondria, typically isolated from unaffected muscles, which are directly injected into the compromised zone. It has been observed that mitochondria are capable of penetrating tissues and cells by passing through the cell membrane. Once inside the cells, they contribute to energy metabolism, potentially promoting a balanced mtDNA state and facilitating the recovery of IRI-affected hearts [ , ]. Skin cells and their mitochondria are significantly impacted by ultraviolet radiation (UVR) and other factors that accelerate premature aging, which can adversely affect the regenerative capacity of the skin [ , , , ]. Addressing skin aging and wounds, the application of AMT/T has been proposed as a potential therapeutic approach, which involves the direct injection of healthy mitochondria to revitalize the affected cells and tissues. It has been observed that the administration of mitochondria in surgical wounds using a mouse model resulted in improved collagen organization and enhanced wound closure [ , ]. By transferring healthy mitochondria, the aim is to counteract the effects of aging and promote tissue regeneration in the skin. Enhancing the delivery of mitochondria to affected cells and tissues is an area of significant interest in the field [ ]. By transferring healthy mitochondria, the aim is to counteract the effects of aging and promote tissue regeneration in the skin. Enhancing the delivery of mitochondria to affected cells and tissues is an area of significant interest in the field [ ]. Researchers are actively developing innovative platforms to ensure the precise and effective delivery of highly functional mitochondria [ ]. These advancements include improvements in isolation techniques, encapsulation methods, and transplantation approaches [ , ]. These advancements in AMT/T have the potential to open up new therapeutic possibilities for a range of diseases in fields such as obstetrics, respiratory medicine, cardiovascular health, central nervous system disorders, immunology, dermatology, conditions like intrauterine growth restriction, and even viral infections like COVID-19 [ ]. The development of improved delivery methods for mitochondria holds promise for expanding the scope of mitochondrial therapy and exploring its applications in various medical fields. The development of mitochondria as an LD holds tremendous promise for the treatment of genetic mitochondrial-related disorders, chronic diseases, wounds, and aging. Techniques like Mitochondrial Augmentation Therapy (MAT) and MitoCeption offer versatile approaches for delivering exogenous mitochondria to cells, showing promising results in improving mitochondrial function and alleviating symptoms in various diseases. Furthermore, the investigation of AMT/T for IRI and its potential for skin regeneration highlights the broad range of medical needs that can benefit from AMT/T therapies. Continued advancements in identifying novel and best sources of mitochondria, isolation techniques, scaling up mitochondria production by bioreactors, or designating certain cells for isolation, transfer, and transplantation approaches will further enhance the delivery of functional mitochondria, expanding the therapeutic possibilities [ , , , , , , , , , , – ]. With ongoing research and development, mitochondria may indeed become a transformative LD with the potential to reshape the landscape of ATMPs and SCTMPs. 6. Conclusions We live at the doorstep of an important and transitional period where commonly used drugs such as druggable molecules will share the therapeutic space with LDs. LDs are able to proliferate, adapt, and respond dynamically to external environments ( ). These entities, sourced from various anatomical origins, may undergo precise genetic engineering and ex-vivo cultivation to impart therapeutic effects or novel capabilities within treated organisms ( ). LDs are characterized by their adaptability, enabling tailored solutions to individual patient needs. However, regulatory agencies still lack a proper framework and definitions to characterize the isolation, modification, expansion, collection and administration of ATMPs. This leads to a more complex classification such as mixing CAR T cells with properties between GTMPs and SCTMPs. Our definition should be considered to build a consensus regarding how to develop and market not only different ATMPs but mitochondria as well ( – ). In this article, we define LDs as novel biological agents that go beyond SCTMPs in the context of ATMPs. LDs encompass cells or subcellular components, such as mitochondria, that are isolated from any anatomical tissue, cultured, and expanded ( – ). These LDs are susceptible to modification to induce a transient or permanent therapeutic effect, improve function, or achieve gain-of-function. As LDs are currently undergoing testing in both preclinical and clinical settings, it is essential to develop new regulations that encompass mitochondria, as well as other components like microvesicles (MVs), as LDs. LDs, such as MSCs, CAR T cells, and mitochondria, possess the ability to induce functional changes and repair cells and tissues, potentially slowing down the decay in an organism. These key properties have shown significant investor and industry interest [ ]. Among LDs, MSCs and CAR T cells are widely recognized. However, their popularity has led to a proliferation of studies lacking the necessary quality standards and scientific rigor, overwhelming the field and hampering their development in the clinic [ ]. The biology and therapeutic use of MSCs, for instance, have generated approximately 75,000 publications. The sheer volume of data on MSCs makes it challenging for researchers to identify relevant evidence for therapy development [ ]. CAR T cells, on the other hand, are isolated (autologous or allogeneic), cultured, expanded in vitro, and genetically engineered to be introduced into the recipient’s body to target cancer cells [ ]. Despite the encouraging outcomes observed with CAR T cells and mitochondria as LDs, it is crucial to understand key aspects of their biology, how they may impact patient safety (toxicities), and therapeutic outcomes to facilitate further development and global accessibility for patients [ , ]. CAR T cells, on the other hand, are isolated (autologous or allogeneic), cultured, expanded in vitro, and genetically engineered to be introduced into the recipient’s body to target cancer cells [ ]. Despite the encouraging outcomes observed with CAR T cells and mitochondria as LDs, it is crucial to understand key aspects of their biology, how they may impact patient safety (toxicities), and therapeutic outcomes to facilitate further development and global accessibility for patients [ , ]. Both MSCs and CAR T cells, whether used in allogeneic or autologous applications, originate from heterogeneous cell sources, leading to variations in their cellular and molecular characteristics, which may also lead to distinct effects among patients. The divergent therapeutic outcomes observed with these LDs motivate researchers to identify the optimal cell source or type that can be replicated, allowing for standardized protocols and effects [ , ]. Academic institutions and companies involved in the development of mitochondria as LDs should learn from the successes and failures of MSCs and CAR T cells by building upon preclinical and clinical evidence, industry quality standards, and regulatory requirements to ensure progress in this field. Further research is needed to better understand how LDs induce their effects and under which conditions. Currently, knowledge has been generated regarding the interindividual effects of MSCs and CAR T cells, as well as possible options to address these issues, including pooling cells or using computational models to predict patient outcomes [ , , ]. Several factors may influence the MSCs’ capacity to induce their regenerative/reparative effects, including differences induced by the immune system [ – ]. Furthermore, the development of LDs, especially mitochondria, should consider their interactions when combined with other drugs. These two aspects are still lacking for most LDs and mitochondria. The adjustments of the drug, dosage, and method of administration should be based on evidence generated from clinical trials and other sources. Addressing these key points is crucial as we continue to gain more knowledge about the mechanisms of action of mitochondria as LDs. We conducted a review of recent and pertinent evidence regarding the therapeutic effects of mitochondria as LDs and the industry’s interest in further exploring and developing their regenerative properties. Several challenges are noted: 1) A need for GMP-grade mitochondria for AMT/T, 2) understanding the optimal source for isolating mitochondria, 3) determining the appropriate dosing and route of administration to ensure therapeutic efficacy, 4) scaling up production while maintaining their functionality and purity over time, and 5) establishing methods to identify diseases and patients suitable for AMT/T is crucial. Additionally, the accessibility of LDs to all patients, scalability, production, and responsiveness to public needs are crucial considerations. The isolation of mitochondria from healthy tissues or cultured cells may impose limitations on scalability. It is important to note that these challenges are not exclusive to mitochondria but are relevant to all cell therapy agents. Notably, the emerging evidence mentioned previously has propelled advancements in the field. Various companies have introduced innovative approaches within the realm of advanced medicinal therapies and technologies. These approaches range from direct administration of mitochondria to the site of injury to ex-vivo manipulations in host cells, such as hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs), followed by re-administration to the patient. These efforts are contributing to the exploration and expansion of mitochondrial LD applications in the field of regenerative medicine. One notable characteristic of LDs is the possession of their own DNA. This DNA can undergo genetic and epigenetic modifications to standardize or enhance their therapeutic effects and outcomes. In the case of mitochondria as LDs, they could translate their own genes in the recipient cell after AMT/T ( – ) [ ]. However, identifying the most suitable genes for inducing such modifications and achieving improvement or functional enhancement remains a significant barrier [ ]. A potential solution to this challenge could involve the development of synthetic cells that contain the necessary genes to optimize LDs’ specific therapeutic functions. The creation of synthetic cells with defined roles has been advancing in recent years, increasing their characteristics and functionality [ ]. However, the complexity arises when synthetic LDs interact with other cells in a normal or pathological microenvironment, posing immense challenges in signal processing and decision-making [ ]. Undoubtedly, synthetic cells, including synthetic mitochondria, will become available as LDs in the future. The progress in this field will heavily rely on interdisciplinary collaboration between cell biology and bioinformatics [ ]. The synergy between these disciplines will contribute to advancements in LD research and pave the way for innovative therapeutic approaches. Interestingly, mitochondrial DNA has been detected extracellularly in various conditions associated with overweight, aging, and other factors. However, the state of this DNA, whether it is packed inside viable or defective mitochondria derived from apoptosis, is still under discussion [ , , ]. The potential application of mitochondria as LDs for treating various conditions, including degenerative diseases, could represent a groundbreaking advancement in the field of cell therapy [ , , , , ]. Notably, even before fully uncovering their therapeutic potential, patents have been filed for products based on mitochondria. A search on Google, Espacenet, and PatentScope databases reveal the existence of patents that encompass a wide range of applications of mitochondria in the treatment of various conditions. These conditions include aging, hair loss, renal, liver, pancreatic, brain, muscle, ocular, and primary mitochondrial diseases [ – , – ]. Other patents involve methods for inducing angiogenesis, producing stem cells enriched with functional mitochondria, utilizing these cells and compositions in therapeutic treatments, and preventing and treating skin damage through the administration of compositions containing intact mitochondria, ruptured mitochondria, and/or mitochondrial constituents, among other applications [ – ]. Additional patents cover methods for isolating mitochondria, treating heart failures, cancer, and damage associated with ischemia-reperfusion injury (IRI), and using enhanced stem and immune cells with mitochondria to treat cancer, infectious diseases, and autoimmune diseases [ – ]. These patents are related to compositions comprising isolated mitochondria or combined mitochondrial agents, aerosolized formulations, methods of use, products, methods for isolating mitochondria, and automated isolation of viable mitochondria. This significant industry effort to secure patents for diverse mitochondrial applications has likely exerted pressure on AMT/T companies to develop innovative solutions. The drive to protect intellectual property rights and secure commercial advantages has likely fostered the development of novel approaches in harnessing the therapeutic potential of mitochondria. These patent applications and the corresponding research and development efforts signify the growing recognition of mitochondria as a valuable resource in the field of regenerative medicine. More research is essential in order to gain a deeper understanding of the potential applications of mitochondria as LDs, ensuring their safety and effectiveness. Comprehensive investigations into preclinical data can offer valuable insights into various aspects such as optimal application methods, dosing, preservation techniques, safety considerations, scalability, isolation procedures, extract purity, and long-term preservation of mitochondria [ ]. By conducting research, we can pave the way for categorizing mitochondria-based therapies into three main drug categories: over-the-counter, behind-the-counter, and prescription-only medicines. This classification system could be based on the specific indications, safety profile, and level of medical supervision required for their use. Ultimately, by gathering robust scientific evidence on the use of mitochondria as an LD, we can determine their appropriate placement within the drug regulatory framework. This will facilitate the development and accessibility of mitochondria-based therapies, ensuring that they are used safely and effectively to benefit patients across a wide range of medical conditions.
